newsitem.title: USA: U.S. black farmers protest over "unfair treatment".
newsitem.headline: U.S. black farmers protest over "unfair treatment".

text.p: Two hundred of America's dwindling number of black farmers marched in the rain Wednesday to demand better treatment from the Agriculture Department and were assured dozens of lawmakers supported them.

Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, who appeared with the farmers at a hearing called by the Congressional Black Caucus, said he was aware of discrimination in his department's lending and farm support programmes.
"Clearly, it does (exist)," he said in prepared remarks.
The farmers complained there was little to show from promises by the department to eradicate illegal bias.
Only two civil rights complaints filed by black farmers have been settled since December, said John Boyd, president of the National Black Farmers Assocation, sponsor of the protest.
"We need change. We need it today," Boyd said at the demonstration in front of Agriculture Department headquarters. "We need to get some emergency (operating) funds so they can plant."
There are fewer than 20,000 black farmers, or less than one percent of about two million farmers in the United States. In 1920, 14 percent of farmers were black.

"Discrimination and lack of access to capital are the key reasons for the decline of the African American farm," said Representative Maxine Waters, California Democrat who chairs the caucus. At current rates, black farms would vanish in a few years, she said in opening the caucus' hearing.
House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt, of Missouri, said that Democratic lawmakers wanted equal treatment for all farmers.
"The entire Democratic caucus (in the House) will stand by you," Gephardt told the farmers.

In February, Glickman announced a campaign to fight racial bias at the department including speedy settling of complaints filed by minority farmers. Some 241 complaints were pending, most of them more than a year old, at that point.
In a memorandum distributed to employees shortly before the rally, Glickman said all civil rights complaints, whether from farmers or agency employees, would be settled by June 6.

The two "major financial settlements" with farmers over loan discrimination "underscore my commitment that USDA stands ready to resolve, quickly and fairly, legitimate civil rights complaints," he wrote.

Glickman also pointed to regulations issued this week to freeze the loan foreclosure process as soon as a civil rights complaint is filed. In the past, only foreclosure sales were halted by such a complaint.
Legislation was being drafted to carry out several reforms including a federal takeover of 12,000 county employees who run the local Agriculture Department offices, he said.
